text: You're the newest hire on the infrastructure team at Briarcliff Systems, and your lead asks you to stand up one Linux VM inside the company's existing Azure virtual network. Every piece of this request maps to something earlier in this course — the VNet, the subnet, the security group, and SSH key-based login. This lesson walks through doing it for real, start to finish.

Three decisions come before the VM ever exists. The VM belongs in the internal app subnet, 10.20.1.0/24, not the public-facing one, because it has no reason to be reachable from the internet. The network security group needs one inbound rule for port 22, scoped to Briarcliff's own office range, not opened to the whole world. And you generate an SSH key pair locally, so there's no password to set, guess, or leak in the first place.

You generate the key pair with ssh-keygen, which produces a private key that stays on your laptop and a public key you hand to Azure. The VM — an Ubuntu Server 22.04 instance — gets created into the app subnet with that public key already installed for the azureuser account, so password authentication for SSH stays disabled from the very first boot.

With the VM running and its public IP assigned, connecting is one line: ssh with your private key, to azureuser at that address. For the session to succeed, three things all have to line up at once — your private key matching the installed public key, the NSG rule letting traffic from Briarcliff's office range through, and sshd actually running on the VM, started automatically by systemd at boot.

A VM that boots isn't automatically a VM that's ready, so before you hand it back you run a short checklist. Systemctl status sshd confirms the service itself is active, not just that the port happens to be open. Apt update and upgrade brings the package index and any security patches current. And a look at /var/log/auth.log confirms the only login so far is your own.

Only after that checklist do you call the VM genuinely done, not just reachable. Next, lesson 32 takes a VM just like this one and asks the harder question: what do you actually check, in what order, when a ticket says it can't be reached at all?
